title: Terraform Providers and Resources
subtitle: How providers connect Terraform to platforms and resources describe managed objects

nodes.label: Provider
nodes.definition: A provider is Terraform's integration layer for a platform or service.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform needs providers to talk to systems like AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Datadog, or other APIs.
nodes.safeSentence: A provider is the bridge between Terraform and the platform being managed.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse the provider with the resource. The provider connects; the resource is the thing being managed.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Providers let Terraform interact with external platforms by calling their APIs.

note.summary:
Terraform does not natively know every platform API. Providers add that knowledge.

Plain-English picture:
Terraform says: manage an AWS S3 bucket.
AWS provider knows: which API calls create/update that bucket.

image.caption: Provider and resource flow from Terraform configuration to real platform objects.

nodes.label: AWS Provider
nodes.definition: The AWS provider lets Terraform manage AWS resources.
nodes.whyItMatters: AWS is a common target for Terraform in data engineering, cloud, platform, and observability work.
nodes.safeSentence: The AWS provider allows Terraform to create and manage AWS infrastructure through code.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not say AWS provider means Terraform runs inside AWS. It means Terraform can talk to AWS APIs.
nodes.interviewAnswer: The AWS provider is the Terraform plugin that knows how to manage AWS services such as S3, IAM, VPC, EC2, Lambda, and CloudWatch.

note.summary: For Sean's context, AWS provider is relevant for S3, IAM, networking, CloudWatch, Lambda, and data-platform resources managed as code.

nodes.label: Provider Configuration
nodes.definition: Provider configuration tells Terraform how to connect to the target platform.
nodes.whyItMatters: The provider needs settings such as region, credentials source, or other connection details.
nodes.safeSentence: Provider configuration tells Terraform how to connect to the platform.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not hardcode secrets directly into provider configuration.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Provider configuration defines connection settings such as the AWS region and how Terraform should authenticate.

nodes.label: Provider Version
nodes.definition: Provider versions control which provider plugin release Terraform uses.
nodes.whyItMatters: Version constraints help keep behavior predictable across machines and teams.
nodes.safeSentence: Provider version constraints help teams avoid surprise behavior changes.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not leave important provider versions completely uncontrolled in team projects.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Provider versions should be managed so Terraform behavior is repeatable across developers and automation.

nodes.label: Resource
nodes.definition: A resource is an infrastructure object Terraform manages.
nodes.whyItMatters: Resources are the things Terraform creates, updates, tracks, or destroys.
nodes.safeSentence: A resource is the infrastructure object Terraform manages.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not think resources are only servers. A resource can be storage, IAM, networking, monitoring, dashboards, alerts, and more.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Resources are the actual infrastructure objects described in Terraform configuration and tracked through state.

note.summary: Examples: S3 bucket, IAM role, VPC, security group, EC2, Lambda, CloudWatch log group, Datadog monitor.

nodes.label: Resource Type
nodes.definition: The resource type says what kind of object Terraform manages.
nodes.whyItMatters: The type tells Terraform and the provider what platform object is being declared.
nodes.safeSentence: The resource type tells Terraform what kind of infrastructure object is being managed.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse resource type with local name.
nodes.interviewAnswer: In a resource block, the type identifies the platform object, such as an S3 bucket or IAM role.

note.summary: Example: in resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs", aws_s3_bucket is the resource type.

nodes.label: Resource Name
nodes.definition: The resource name is the local Terraform name used inside the configuration.
nodes.whyItMatters: The local name lets other Terraform code refer to this resource.
nodes.safeSentence: The local resource name lets other parts of the Terraform code reference that object.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not assume the local Terraform name is always the real cloud resource name.
nodes.interviewAnswer: The local name is Terraform's internal name for referencing a resource in the configuration.

note.summary: In resource "aws_s3_bucket" "logs", logs is local Terraform name. Real bucket name may be different.

nodes.label: Resource Address
nodes.definition: A resource address is Terraform's full reference to a managed object in the configuration and state.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform uses addresses to connect configuration, state, and operations.
nodes.safeSentence: A resource address is Terraform's way of naming a managed object.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse a resource address with the cloud provider's resource ID.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform uses resource addresses like aws_s3_bucket.logs to identify managed objects in code and state.

note.summary: Address format combines type + local name, e.g., aws_s3_bucket.logs. This is key for state mapping and operations.

nodes.label: Attributes
nodes.definition: Attributes are values exposed by resources or data sources.
nodes.whyItMatters: Attributes allow Terraform objects to connect to each other.
nodes.safeSentence: Attributes let Terraform pass values from one object to another.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not hardcode values when Terraform can reference attributes safely.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Attributes expose useful values, such as IDs, names, ARNs, URLs, or endpoints, so other resources can reference them.

note.summary: Example pattern: one resource exports an ID, another resource references that attribute. This supports dependency inference.

nodes.label: Data Source
nodes.definition: A data source reads existing information instead of creating a new resource.
nodes.whyItMatters: Data sources let Terraform use existing infrastructure or platform facts.
nodes.safeSentence: Data sources let Terraform look up existing information without creating it.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not confuse data sources with resources. Resources manage objects; data sources read objects.
nodes.interviewAnswer: A data source is used when Terraform needs to look up existing information, such as an existing VPC, AMI, account identity, or policy document.

note.summary: Plain English: Resource = create/manage this. Data source = look this up and use it.

nodes.label: Dependencies
nodes.definition: Dependencies define ordering between Terraform objects.
nodes.whyItMatters: Terraform needs to know what must exist before something else can be created.
nodes.safeSentence: Terraform often infers dependency order from references.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not overuse manual depends_on when normal references already show the dependency.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Terraform usually infers dependencies when one resource references another, so it can build things in the right order.

note.summary: If an EC2 instance references a security group ID attribute, Terraform knows security group must be created first.

nodes.label: Terraform 1000-Foot View
nodes.definition: Open the map that explains Terraform's basic mental model.
nodes.whyItMatters: This gives Sean a doorway back to the big-picture Terraform map.
nodes.safeSentence: Providers and resources make more sense when connected back to the 1000-foot Terraform model.
nodes.commonTrap: Do not mix this navigation bubble with provider/resource concepts. It is a map doorway.
nodes.interviewAnswer: Providers and resources are two central parts of the Terraform model: providers connect to platforms, and resources describe what gets managed.
